question: You are building the observability stack for a platform. Why are metrics the foundational layer, and what types of metrics should you collect?
answer: Metrics are numeric time-series data that are cheap to store, fast to query, and enable real-time alerting. Collect three types: 1) RED metrics per service — request Rate, Error rate, Duration (latency). 2) USE metrics per resource — Utilization, Saturation, Errors for CPU, memory, disk, network. 3) Business metrics — signups, orders, revenue. Prometheus is the standard: applications expose /metrics endpoints, Prometheus scrapes them, and stores them as time-series.

question: Metrics tell you something is wrong. Why do you also need logs, and what makes logs useful for debugging?
answer: Metrics show patterns and aggregates (error rate = 5%) but not specifics (which request failed and why). Logs provide the detailed context: the exact error message, stack trace, request parameters, user ID, and correlation ID. Structured logs (JSON with consistent fields) are searchable and parseable. Every log line should include: timestamp, severity level, service name, trace ID, and a human-readable message. Logs answer "what exactly happened" after metrics show "something is wrong."

question: Logs show an error in one service, but the request touched 5 services. How do distributed traces help you follow a request across services?
answer: Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Tempo) assigns a unique trace ID to each request at the entry point. As the request flows through services, each service creates a span (a timed operation) linked to the trace ID. The trace shows the complete request path: which services were called, in what order, how long each took, and where errors occurred. This is essential for diagnosing latency in microservices — you can see that service-C took 2 seconds because it was waiting on service-D's database query.

question: You have metrics, logs, and traces in separate systems. How do you correlate them to diagnose a single incident efficiently?
answer: Link all three signals using shared identifiers: 1) Exemplars in Prometheus link metrics to specific trace IDs (click a latency spike to see the trace). 2) Trace IDs in log lines let you search logs for a specific request (search by trace_id=abc123). 3) Dashboards link panels: click a metric anomaly to jump to filtered logs for that time window and service. Grafana supports this natively: metrics panel → click data point → jump to Tempo trace → jump to Loki logs with the same trace ID. This reduces investigation time from hours to minutes.

question: Signals are correlated. How do you build dashboards that provide actionable insight instead of noise?
answer: Design dashboards in layers: 1) Overview dashboard: the 4 golden signals for all services at a glance — spotting which service is unhealthy. 2) Per-service dashboards: detailed RED metrics, resource utilization, dependencies. 3) Infrastructure dashboards: node health, disk, network. Key principles: show rates not totals (req/sec not total requests), use percentiles not averages (p99 latency, not mean), highlight anomalies (threshold lines, red/green coloring), include time selectors for comparison. Every graph should answer a question.

question: Dashboards exist. How do you design alerts that are actionable and avoid alert fatigue?
answer: Alert on symptoms (user-facing impact), not causes (CPU utilization). Every alert must have: 1) A clear condition (error rate > 1% for 5 minutes). 2) A severity level driving the response (critical = page, warning = Slack). 3) A runbook link with exact steps to diagnose and fix. 4) Context in the notification (which service, current value, dashboard link). Remove alerts that fire frequently but require no action. Test alerts regularly (fire drills). Track alert metrics: alerts per week, false positive rate, time to acknowledge.

question: Alerts fire on thresholds. How do SLOs and error budgets provide a more principled approach to alerting?
answer: Define SLOs based on user experience: "99.9% of requests complete within 500ms." The error budget is the allowed failure rate: 0.1% = 43.2 minutes/month. Alert on burn rate: how fast you are consuming the budget. A 14.4x burn rate means you will exhaust the monthly budget in 2 days — that warrants a page. Multi-window alerts (1h fast burn AND 6h slow burn) catch both spikes and slow degradations. Error budgets align engineering priorities: when budget is exhausted, prioritize reliability over features.

question: Your service consumed 80% of its monthly error budget in the first week. What operational decisions does this drive?
answer: 1) Freeze non-essential deployments — new changes risk burning remaining budget. 2) Prioritize reliability work: investigate and fix the root cause of the budget burn. 3) Review recent changes for the source of increased errors. 4) Tighten deployment practices (mandatory canary, smaller batches). 5) If budget is exhausted, implement a formal feature freeze until reliability improves. 6) Report to stakeholders: "we have X minutes of error budget remaining this month." Error budgets create a shared language between engineering and product for reliability trade-offs.

question: Looking at the full observability stack, how do you use observability data to drive continuous improvement?
answer: 1) Weekly review: analyze top errors, slowest endpoints, most-paged services. 2) Monthly trends: are error rates improving or worsening? Are SLOs being met? 3) Postmortem action tracking: did the fix actually reduce the alert frequency? 4) Capacity planning: use utilization trends to forecast growth. 5) Performance optimization: trace analysis reveals the slowest dependencies. 6) Cost optimization: identify over-provisioned services via low utilization metrics. Observability is not just for incidents — it is the feedback loop that drives all operational improvement.
